summary:
American Samoa is an unincorporated United States territory and stands under the United States federal framework. Executive measures adopted in January 2025 on binary sex classification in identity documents, federal facilities, care funding and athletic participation reach the territory through federal agencies operating here. Federal identity documents issued to residents follow that regime: new and renewed passports record sex assigned at birth, the X marker introduced in 2022 is no longer issued, applications are processed only as M or F on the basis of supporting documents, and passports already carrying an X marker remain valid until expiry.

Same-sex marriage is not licensed in American Samoa. The territory's Attorney General began reviewing in July 2015 whether the United States Supreme Court's marriage-equality ruling applied locally, and the Governor stated at the time that it did not, citing the territory's preamble, its constitution, Christian values and its unorganised and unincorporated political status. No same-sex couple has applied for a marriage licence in the territory.

A 2026 law review article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa concludes that the 2015 ruling does apply despite those official statements, and that the territory would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied. The article sets out the litigation route: the High Court of American Samoa first, with the Territorial Registrar as defendant, then the United States Department of the Interior. Reporting from the territory in July 2024 described the local ban as still treated as operative on the island and its durability under the Fourteenth Amendment as an open question, with a survey by a constitutional and comparative law professor testing the issue.

Since 13 December 2022 the federal Respect for Marriage Act has obliged American Samoa to recognise, with equal treatment, same-sex marriages performed lawfully in another jurisdiction, without requiring performance here. The sources describe American Samoa as the only United States jurisdiction, alongside certain tribal jurisdictions, still enforcing a ban on same-sex couples marrying.

The Fono Senate rejected a bill on 20 March 2003 that would have outlawed same-sex marriage, after the House Judiciary Committee recommended it be killed. The sponsor, Representative Sua Carl Schuster, sought to preempt the marriage litigation then unfolding in United States states. At the committee hearing fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that Samoan fa'afafine do not seek marriage with other men, describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech and citing Christian upbringing. In January 2016 the Senate unanimously confirmed former Attorney General Fiti Alexander Sunia as a District Court judge after he told the confirmation hearing that he had not read the 2015 Supreme Court decision, that the district court does not deal with it, and that he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws change.

Consensual sodomy has not been a criminal offence since the 1979 revision of the criminal law took effect in 1980, which retained prohibition only for public acts, prostitution, minors and persons unable to consent. The first sodomy statute, enacted in 1963, criminalised male homosexual and heterosexual conduct and did not address lesbian sex. The age of consent is 16, regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

Fa'afafine, boys raised as girls to take an important domestic role in Samoan communal life, are described in the sources as a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture, and the territory supports an organised community presence. Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (SOFIAS) was formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, runs annual events and campaigns for the fa'afafine community, and the first Pride festival was held in August 2016 in Utulei with pageant, song, dance and poetry competitions. Beauty pageants among the fa'afafine community are popular and families generally attend in numbers.

American Samoan society is nonetheless highly religious, and conservative attitudes on gender and sexuality tend to dominate. Reserved public behaviour is expected of people of all orientations, and open displays of affection between couples, same-sex or opposite-sex, may offend.

Protection machinery has been used locally. In September 2023 the United States Justice Department secured a settlement with the American Samoa Government resolving an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee, following a June 2023 federal civil action that cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity. In February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teen.
tangentialFactors:
A 2009 travel advice column describes Samoan culture as tending toward traditionalism, with reserved behaviour expected of people of all orientations, while reporting homosexuality as widely accepted in Samoan culture in contrast to Fiji, and describing fa'afafine courtship of Western visitors. A local artist calls the Samoan islands the homeland of fa'afafine culture. The territory's roughly 57,000 residents live across seven islands and atolls, and its hotels skew toward business travel in Pago Pago.

A University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa research guide on Pacific sexual identity, last updated 23 July 2026, defines fa'afafine as born male but embodying both male and female traits and a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture, and frames the community's organisations within a pattern of colonial suppression followed by contemporary reclaiming of Pacific gender identities. The neighbouring independent state of Samoa is described as similarly tolerant of transgender people and identities.

The July 2024 survey on the local marriage ban also probes cultural dimensions bearing on the question, including collectivistic versus individualistic orientation and linear versus polychronic time, which the sources treat as relevant to how a constitutional challenge would be received.
localsOnly:
The High Court of American Samoa has held that birth certificates should only be altered to correct information that was erroneous at the time of recordation or to reflect a name change due to adoption, and the Office of Vital Statistics has interpreted that ruling to cover applications from transgender individuals. The Office will change the name on a birth certificate when presented with a name change order, and may change the gender marker with medical documentation of the sex change.

The American Samoa Code does not specify the sex of the parties to a marriage; it refers to the age of the male and the female and prescribes a form in which parties identify as son and as daughter. Residents therefore marry under a statutory text written in binary terms while the territory declines to license same-sex marriages, even as marriages performed elsewhere must be recognised and treated equally under federal law since 13 December 2022.

Community infrastructure for fa'afafine and LGBTQ residents centres on Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa, which organises annual events and festivals and campaigns for the fa'afafine community, alongside the Pride festival first held in Utulei in August 2016. Residents also face the everyday expectation of reserved conduct in public and a strongly religious social environment.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2015 federal marriage ruling is operative in American Samoa is contested in the sources rather than settled: a 2026 legal analysis says it applies and that a certificate must be issued on application, while territorial officials have said it does not and the local ban is still treated as operative. Because no same-sex couple has filed a licence application, the question has never been tested in practice, and whether the ban would survive a Fourteenth Amendment challenge remains unresolved.

No territory-specific source in the inventory addresses airport screening, border or entry screening, restroom or facility access, or healthcare provision for trans visitors in American Samoa; the document rules cited here are sourced from national reporting and national legal guidance rather than from territorial agencies.

The inventory contains no trans-specific violence or killing statistics for American Samoa, so no comparison against the territory's general homicide rate can be made and none is implied. The February 2023 sexual abuse charge is a single documented incident, not a measured rate.
